subject: inputing aggregated binned data into Distance

messages.author: f2b3eb601db76d8e
messages.subject: inputing aggregated binned data into Distance
parts:
Hello,


I am trying to read the aggregated, binned count data into "Distance" R wrapper. The data come from multiple transects surveyed once, with bird counts provided as totals for 4 distance bands. I.e.  for each transect I have four figures representing totals for each of the four distance bands. 


Sample.Label    band1   band2   band3   band4

BA.601                 6             300         34           7


As far as I can see from the "Distance" vignette (Miller et al on bioRxiv), input for "Distance" assumes each record is observation of a single bird (plus associated info on distance band). Is there any way to read the grouped data like this into "Distance"? With a total of say 300 birds recorded for distance band #2, I should probably generate 300 separate records with attributes of this band, which seems a lot of unnecessary work. Is there any way to get around this problem and to seamlessly input the aggregated data from binned distance bands into "Distance" - within R? I have not been using DISTANCE sa the Win/stand alone program (obviously) and try to stay within R environment if possible.


Best wishes,

Przemek Chylarecki

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] inputing aggregated binned data into Distance
parts:
Przemek

Detecting 300 birds in a band from a single point is quite impressive.

Nevertheless, you can get your distance data ready for analysis using the ds() function with a bit of crafty R code, employing the rep() function.  I have used the information you provided for a single point, and manufactured the cutpoints for your bands as you did not provide them.  Perhaps from the example I have provided you can extend it to accommodate the remainder of your stations.

library(Distance)
band.midpoints <- c(5,30,75,125)  # these are artificial
cuts <- c(0,10,50,100,150)  # also artificial, matching the midpoints above
bands <- c(6,300,34,7)  # for this single station
tot.birds <- sum(bands)
this.label <- rep("BA.601", times=tot.birds)
dists <- c(rep(band.midpoints, times=bands))
my.data <- data.frame(Sample.Label=this.label, distance=dists)
my.result <- ds(my.data, transect="point", cutpoints=cuts, key="hn", adjustment=NULL)
plot(my.result, pdf=TRUE)

Thank you very much for the code that allowed me to migrate my data into Distance. Hopefully, it will be useful also for other folks wanting to move the data from unmarked::distsamp() to Distance::ds().
After all, I forget to mention that my data refer to line transects rather than point transects, representing counts of marine ducks wintering offshore. So, 300 birds in second distance band are still within the limits of 'normal' observations here (unlike 300 birds recorded during the point count:-).
Again, many thanks,
Best wishes,
Przemek

messages.author: 44f1f9ea3d910e12
messages.subject: AW: [distance-sampling] inputing aggregated binned data into Distance
parts:
Hi Przemek,

 

that is what I guessed when reading your question – so you would better not enter the 347 ducks as single birds, because you probably have observed clusters of birds. Cluster size is usually an important covariate when estimating ESW in seaducks.

 

In addition you have a serious problem with ducks moving from the transect line, or the way you (or probably someone else) assigned them to bands, or with the vessel you were working on. Merging the inner bands 1+2 might be an option here.

 

Best wishes

Jochen

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] inputing aggregated binned data into Distance
parts:
Hi Jochen,

You are perfectly right with the flocking as a factor to include in modeling here. The problem is, the data I have got do not have cluster size recorded. Observers usually claim that birds are often dispersed in a way that makes quite difficult to assign them to separate clusters. So, while I wish to try models with clusters, I actually can't do that. The main clustering is probably reflected in another scale - analysis units comprise of quite short line transects, only c.1200 m long. Many of these units (over 40%) are free of birds (focal species) at all. So, I believe, clustering is - to some extent at least - reflected at this level (between units).

Birds moving away from the transect line pose a problem too, obviously. However, the structure of the whole data is not as bad as for that single, exemplary, transect line provided in my post. Overall, 53% of individuals were in the first band, which looks healthy enough:-)). Having said that, I must admit the data are still quite challenging (as you perfectly know;-), as even "best" models, with reasonable estimates still show a dramatic lack of fit.

Thanks for suggestions,
Best wishes,
Przemek
